questions_and_answers.question_text: What does the verb huàn really mean?
What indicates whether to translate huàn as "change into" or "change from"?
Which English verb does the book compare huàn to?
Write the Chinese for "I want to change some money into Taiwan currency."
What does huàn set up between the two items being exchanged?
In the middle of a stay in Taiwan, what would huàn Táibì be assumed to mean?
At the end of a stay in Taiwan, what would huàn Táibì be assumed to mean?
Write the Chinese for "One U.S. dollar is thirty-eight dollars in Taiwan currency."

articles.text:
6. A: Wǒ yào huàn yìdiǎn Táibì.      I want to change some money into
      Zhè shi yìbǎikuài Měijīnde     Taiwan currency. Here are one
      lǚxíng zhīpiào.                hundred U.S. dollars in traveler's
                                     checks.
   C: Hǎo. Yíkuài Měijīn huàn        Certainly. One U.S. dollar is
      sānshibākuài Táibì.            thirty-eight dollars in Taiwan
                                     currency.

Note on No. 6

Huàn Táibì: The verb huàn really means "to exchange," that is, to replace one thing with another. Huàn sets up an equivalence between the two items being exchanged but does not indicate the direction of the exchange (i.e., which item the speaker starts with and which he ends up with). In the middle of someone's stay in Taiwan, we assume that the phrase huàn Táibì refers to changing some money INTO Taiwan currency. At the end of a stay in Taiwan, we would guess that the phrase refers to changing money FROM Taiwan currency. Only the context indicates whether to translate huàn as "change into" or as "change from."

(The English verb "rent" is similar: The sentence "I want to rent an apartment" could mean either "I have an apartment to rent TO someone" or "I want to find an apartment to rent FROM someone.")
